title: IBM to End Visa and Green Card Sponsorship for Most IBM Consulting Roles
excerpt: IBM is discontinuing visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of sponsored roles in IBM Consulting, its largest division, Bloomberg reported. Affected workers can keep working for IBM outside the United States, or leave the company at the end of the year, according to an internal document Bloomberg saw.
body:
• IBM is ending immigration sponsorship for some roles in IBM Consulting, its largest division, and discontinuing visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles there, the company told Bloomberg.
  • Workers affected by the change can continue working with IBM outside the United States, or leave the company at the end of the year, according to a document shared with managers this week that Bloomberg saw.
  • The reports do not name other IBM divisions; the announced change is specific to IBM Consulting roles that rely on sponsorship.
  • If you are in an affected role, your immediate steps are to confirm your status in writing with your manager and IBM immigration counsel, and to understand your visa's own deadlines before the end-of-year date in the document.

International Business Machines Corp. is ending immigration sponsorship for some roles in its largest division, following the Trump administration's crackdown on a visa program that has been a talent pipeline for the tech industry, Bloomberg Law reported. The change covers IBM Consulting, which Bloomberg described as by far IBM's largest division.

Who Is Affected

The workers affected are those in IBM Consulting roles that depend on company sponsorship, both for work visas and for green cards. IBM has not, in the reporting, extended the change to its other divisions, and the reports do not suggest that existing visas are cancelled by this decision. Sponsorship is the employer's side of the process: for H-1B status, the employer files the petition (see the USCIS H-1B page), and for most employment-based green cards the employer runs the labor certification and immigrant petition. When an employer stops sponsoring, the worker's route to staying in that role in the US stops with it, even though the worker's current status runs to its own expiry date.

"We have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting."

— IBM spokesperson, quoted by Bloomberg

What Changes, and When

According to a document shared with managers in the division this week and seen by Bloomberg, impacted workers can continue working with IBM outside the US, or leave the company at the end of the year. The reporting does not publish a fuller timetable, a headcount, or a list of the roles that keep sponsorship, and IBM's statement speaks only to the majority of sponsored roles in Consulting. Workers should treat the end of the year as the operative date in the document Bloomberg saw, and get their own position confirmed rather than relying on the general description.

What to Do Next

If you work in IBM Consulting on a sponsored visa or in a sponsored green card process, the practical steps from this reporting are: ask your manager and IBM's immigration counsel, in writing, whether your role is in the discontinued group; ask what internal roles outside the US are open to you, since the document presents that as the alternative to leaving; and take independent immigration advice on your own status, including how long your current visa remains valid and what other US employers or categories could mean for you. Nothing in the reporting changes the validity of a visa already issued, and Bloomberg's coverage frames this as a company policy decision inside one division, not a government order.

The Wider Context

Bloomberg placed the decision against the administration's broader crackdown on the visa programs tech companies use to hire and retain foreign professionals. IBM is one of the largest employers of Indian technology professionals in the United States, and Consulting is the division where client-facing, project-based roles, many of them sponsorship-dependent, are concentrated. Whether other large employers follow with division-level sponsorship cuts is now the open question for the sector.
